A command to wear a sign follows at once, עֲשֵׂ֣ה לְךָ֔ מוֹסֵר֖וֹת וּמֹט֑וֹת וּנְתַתָּ֖ם עַל צַוָּארֶֽךָ (oshb:Jer.27.2, byte), matching “Make bonds and bars, and put them on your neck.” (web:Jer.27.2). The envoys the sign is sent through are said to come אֶל צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה (oshb:Jer.27.3, byte), matching “to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah” (web:Jer.27.3): the reign named at the header and the reign the delivered sign actually reaches diverge, and that divergence is held open here rather than resolved by reading a different king at the header. A single relayed message follows without any change of speaker, opening on the full title stack כֹּֽה אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל (oshb:Jer.27.4, byte), matching “Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says” (web:Jer.27.4); nothing inside verses 5 through 10 reopens that stack with a different speaker, an addressee change, or a fresh discourse imperative, so the whole relayed message stands as one unit. It closes on וְהַגּ֗וֹי אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָבִ֧יא אֶת צַוָּאר֛וֹ בְּעֹ֥ל מֶֽלֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל וַֽעֲבָד֑וֹ (oshb:Jer.27.11, byte), matching “But the nation that brings their neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, that nation I will let remain in their own land,” (web:Jer.27.11). Verse 12 opens a fresh address, וְאֶל צִדְקִיָּ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָה֙ דִּבַּ֔רְתִּי (oshb:Jer.27.12, byte) — from the envoys of five foreign kings to Zedekiah named directly in Jeremiah’s own first-person report — and this row stops short of that turn.

boundary_rationale: An epistolary superscription opens the unit, וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַסֵּ֔פֶר אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁלַ֛ח יִרְמְיָ֥ה הַנָּבִ֖יא מִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם (oshb:Jer.29.1, byte), matching “Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the residue of the elders of the captivity, and to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon,” (web:Jer.29.1) — naming the document itself a letter rather than a spoken oracle, sent from Jerusalem to the exile community by name. It continues through the courier commission, בְּיַד֙ אֶלְעָשָׂ֣ה בֶן שָׁפָ֔ן וּגְמַרְיָ֖ה בֶּן חִלְקִיָּ֑ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר שָׁלַ֜ח צִדְקִיָּ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה אֶל נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֛ר מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל בָּבֶ֥לָה לֵאמֹֽר (oshb:Jer.29.3, byte), matching “by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon). It said:” (web:Jer.29.3), closing on the citation formula that opens the letter’s own quoted content. No koh-amar, addressee shift, or discourse imperative interrupts the superscription itself; it is pure epistolary framing naming sender, recipients, and couriers, with no oracular content of its own. Verse 4 opens the letter’s actual quoted content, addressed in Yahweh’s own voice for the first time, and this row is bounded there.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this superscription into the letter’s own opening instructions as one row was rejected because verses 1 through 3 carry no koh-amar or other speech formula of their own; they name the document, its sender, its recipients, and its couriers before any quoted content begins.
literature_type_guess: epistolary superscription naming sender, recipients, couriers

Nebuchadnezzar’s name recurs in the plene nun-family spelling within this short span (oshb:Jer.29.1, oshb:Jer.29.3), the form that clusters through the letter’s own opening verses before other spellings appear later in the same chapter.

boundary_rationale: The letter’s own quoted content opens on the full title stack, כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל לְכָל הַ֨גּוֹלָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר הִגְלֵ֥יתִי מִירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בָּבֶֽלָה (oshb:Jer.29.4, byte), matching “Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:” (web:Jer.29.4), addressed to all the exiles by name for the first time in the letter. Settle-in instructions follow at once, בְּנ֥וּ בָתִּ֖ים וְשֵׁ֑בוּ וְנִטְע֣וּ גַנּ֔וֹת (oshb:Jer.29.5, byte), matching “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.” (web:Jer.29.5). A further koh-amar recurs at verse 8, turning from settling in to a warning against the exiles’ own prophets and diviners, and a third recurs at verse 10, כִּֽי כֹה֙ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֠י לְפִ֞י מְלֹ֧את לְבָבֶ֛ל שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה אֶפְקֹ֣ד (oshb:Jer.29.10, byte), matching “After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.” (web:Jer.29.10) — a promise of return after seventy years; none of these internal recurrences carries a change of speaker or a fresh addressee of its own, so all three turns are held inside one continuous letter-address to the same audience rather than cut into separate rows. It closes on “and I will turn again your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places where I have driven you,” (web:Jer.29.14); a ketiv/qere note sits in this same closing verse, on the word for captivity itself: ketiv שביתכם against qere שְׁבוּתְכֶ֗ם (oshb:Jer.29.14, WLC, single-witness). The address turns from Yahweh’s own promise to a claim quoted from the exiles’ own mouths at verse 15, marking the far edge of this row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting fresh rows at the koh-amar recurrences opening verses 8 and 10 was considered, since each turns to a distinct topic within the letter — the false prophets, then the seventy-year promise — but rejected because none carries a frame-owner change or an addressee shift of its own; the whole eleven-verse span remains one sustained address from Yahweh to the same exile audience, held together honestly rather than split on topic alone.
literature_type_guess: the letter’s opening instructions and restoration promise

The whole span sits inside Jeremiah’s letter, disclosed here as its embedding frame rather than argued as this row’s own operative category, which follows the restoration promise that dominates its closing verses.

boundary_rationale: A claim quoted from the exiles’ own mouths opens the unit, כִּ֖י אֲמַרְתֶּ֑ם (oshb:Jer.29.15, byte), matching “Because you have said,” (web:Jer.29.15) — a setumah falls in this same opening verse. The address then turns to a party the letter has not yet named directly, כִּי כֹ֣ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַיּוֹשֵׁב֙ אֶל כִּסֵּ֣א דָוִ֔ד וְאֶל כָּל הָעָ֔ם הַיּוֹשֵׁ֖ב בָּעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֑את אֲחֵיכֶ֕ם אֲשֶׁ֛ר לֹֽא יָצְא֥וּ אִתְּכֶ֖ם בַּגּוֹלָֽה (oshb:Jer.29.16, byte), matching “Yahweh says concerning the king who sits on David’s throne, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your brothers who haven’t gone with you into captivity,” (web:Jer.29.16) — the king on David’s throne and the people who stayed in Jerusalem, rather than the exiles the letter actually addresses. Judgment against them continues through verse 18, matching “I will pursue after them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth, to be an object of horror, an astonishment, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations where I have driven them,” (web:Jer.29.18); a ketiv/qere note sits in this same verse, on the word for horror itself: ketiv לזועה against qere לְזַעֲוָ֜ה (oshb:Jer.29.18, WLC, single-witness). It closes on a summons back to the letter’s own audience, וְאַתֶּ֖ם שִׁמְע֣וּ דְבַר יְהוָ֑ה כָּל הַ֨גּוֹלָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר שִׁלַּ֥חְתִּי מִירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בָּבֶֽלָה (oshb:Jer.29.20, byte), matching “Hear therefore Yahweh’s word, all you captives whom I have sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.” (web:Jer.29.20) — a setumah also falls in this closing verse. Whether verse 15’s quoted claim belongs with the settle-in promise that precedes it or with the Jerusalem judgment it introduces is not settled by any formula; it is read here with what follows, since the address it opens is answered only by the turn to the king and the city at verse 16. A fresh koh-amar names two further parties directly at verse 21, Ahab and Zedekiah, so this row is bounded just short of that naming.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading verse 15 as the closing verse of the settle-in and restoration unit that precedes it, rather than as the opening of the Jerusalem judgment that follows, was seriously considered and is not decided here: no formula marks which side of the seam it belongs on, and the row is held at reduced confidence honestly rather than resolving that question either way.

boundary_rationale: A fresh koh-amar names two further parties directly for the first time, אֶל אַחְאָ֤ב בֶּן קֽוֹלָיָה֙ וְאֶל צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בֶן מַֽעֲשֵׂיָ֔ה (oshb:Jer.29.21, byte), matching “Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and concerning Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who prophesy a lie to you in my name:” (web:Jer.29.21) — Ahab and Zedekiah, prophesying falsely in Yahweh’s name among the exiles themselves. Their sentence names the king who will kill them, בְּיַד֙ נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר (oshb:Jer.29.21, byte) — a resh-family spelling of Nebuchadnezzar’s name, distinct from the nun-family forms spelled earlier in this same letter at oshb:Jer.29.1 and oshb:Jer.29.3. The unit continues through the curse formula built on both their names and closes on the rationale for the sentence, יַ֡עַן אֲשֶׁר֩ עָשׂ֨וּ נְבָלָ֜ה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַיְנַֽאֲפוּ֙ אֶת נְשֵׁ֣י רֵֽעֵיהֶ֔ם וַיְדַבְּר֨וּ דָבָ֤ר בִּשְׁמִי֙ שֶׁ֔קֶר אֲשֶׁ֖ר ל֣וֹא צִוִּיתִ֑ם וְאָנֹכִ֛י (oshb:Jer.29.23, byte), matching “because they have done foolish things in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbors’ wives, and have spoken words in my name falsely, which I didn’t command them. I am he who knows, and am witness,” (web:Jer.29.23); a ketiv/qere note sits in this same closing verse: ketiv הו ידע against qere הַיּוֹדֵ֥עַ (oshb:Jer.29.23, WLC, single-witness), alongside a separate OSHB exegesis note at the same verse (single-witness apparatus, not text bytes). The address turns to a third, differently-named figure at verse 24, Shemaiah the Nehelamite, which is where this row ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the curse-formula of verse 22 from the naming and sentence of verse 21 into its own row was rejected because it is grammatically bound back to Ahab and Zedekiah by name, one continuous judgment rather than a fresh address.

boundary_rationale: A third named figure opens the unit, וְאֶל שְׁמַעְיָ֥הוּ הַנֶּחֱלָמִ֖י תֹּאמַ֥ר לֵאמֹֽר (oshb:Jer.29.24, byte), matching “Concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall speak, saying,” (web:Jer.29.24) — Shemaiah the Nehelamite, commissioned as the subject of Jeremiah’s own reply rather than addressed directly. The reply quotes Shemaiah’s own hostile letter back at him, including its rebuke naming Jeremiah by his home village, בְּיִרְמְיָ֖הוּ הָֽעֲנְּתֹתִ֑י (oshb:Jer.29.27, byte), matching “Now therefore, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who makes himself a prophet to you,” (web:Jer.29.27) — a defective spelling of the gentilic naming that village. It closes on a narrative report explaining how this exchange became known, וַיִּקְרָ֛א צְפַנְיָ֥ה הַכֹּהֵ֖ן אֶת הַסֵּ֣פֶר הַזֶּ֑ה בְּאָזְנֵ֖י יִרְמְיָ֥הוּ הַנָּבִֽיא (oshb:Jer.29.29, byte), matching “Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet.” (web:Jer.29.29). A fresh word-event formula opens at verse 30, turning from this narrative report to Yahweh’s own word to Jeremiah, and the row does not extend past that opening.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing this row at verse 28, immediately after the quoted content of Shemaiah’s own letter, and reading verse 29 as the opening of the row that follows, was rejected because verse 29’s report refers back to this letter by name and completes the account of how it was heard, rather than introducing the fresh word-event formula that actually opens the next unit at verse 30.

A setumah and a doubled paseq both fall in this closing verse.
